clinicalPearls: A rare defect of the Rapoport-Luebering shunt that characteristically causes erythrocytosis rather than haemolytic anaemia
Deficiency lowers red-cell 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate, increasing haemoglobin's oxygen affinity and reducing oxygen release to tissues
The resulting tissue hypoxia drives a compensatory increase in erythropoietin and a secondary polycythaemia
It is an important consideration in the workup of unexplained erythrocytosis with a low 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate and left-shifted oxygen dissociation curve
Inherited as an autosomal recessive trait, so consanguinity or affected relatives may be present
Diagnosis rests on demonstrating a low red-cell 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate, reduced enzyme activity and a BPGM mutation
Management is generally conservative; the erythrocytosis is compensatory and venesection is usually unnecessary and may be counterproductive
reference.pathophysiology: Bisphosphoglycerate mutase drives the Rapoport-Luebering shunt, converting 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate to 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate, the principal regulator of haemoglobin oxygen affinity in the red cell. When the enzyme is deficient, 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate concentrations fall, shifting the oxygen dissociation curve to the left so that haemoglobin binds oxygen more tightly and releases less to the tissues. The consequent tissue hypoxia stimulates erythropoietin and produces a secondary erythrocytosis; because ATP-generating glycolysis is largely preserved, haemolysis is not a prominent feature.
additionalDifferentials: Secondary erythrocytosis from hypoxia or erythropoietin excess
Congenital erythrocytosis from erythropoietin receptor or oxygen-sensing pathway mutations
additionalInvestigations: Full blood count showing erythrocytosis with serum erythropoietin
Haemoglobin variant analysis to exclude a high-affinity variant
Molecular testing of the BPGM gene
redFlags: Symptoms of hyperviscosity from marked erythrocytosis
Thrombotic events attributable to a high haematocrit
Misclassification as polycythaemia vera leading to inappropriate cytoreductive treatment
Inappropriate aggressive venesection worsening tissue oxygen delivery
reference.prognosis: The prognosis is generally good; the erythrocytosis is a compensatory response to increased oxygen affinity and most patients remain well without specific intervention.
pitfalls: Mistaking the compensatory erythrocytosis for polycythaemia vera and treating with cytoreduction
Performing unnecessary or over-aggressive venesection that impairs oxygen delivery
Failing to measure 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate and the oxygen dissociation curve in unexplained erythrocytosis
Overlooking a high-affinity haemoglobin variant as an alternative explanation
management: Reassurance and observation, as the erythrocytosis is a compensatory response to increased haemoglobin oxygen affinity and usually needs no specific treatment
Avoid routine venesection, since reducing the red-cell mass would compromise this physiological compensation for impaired tissue oxygen delivery
Distinguish clearly from polycythaemia vera and other primary erythrocytoses to avoid inappropriate cytoreductive therapy
Attention to general cardiovascular risk factors, with cautious consideration of hyperviscosity only if genuinely symptomatic
Genetic counselling and family screening given autosomal recessive inheritance
Periodic monitoring of the full blood count and symptoms
